agr0: Understanding Pain: How Pain Works and Why It Can Persist | İhsan Eren
agr1: Pain is always real, but its intensity does not always reflect tissue damage. The new definition of pain, the body’s alarm system analogy and the MRI findings of people without pain: an interactive guide.
agr3: Pain is real; always. But how much it hurts does not always reflect how much damage there is in the tissues. The brain weighs the signals coming from the body together with your sleep, stress, fears and past experiences, and makes a decision to protect you. Understanding how pain works can reduce the fear of moving, especially when pain has lasted a long time.

agr11: “An unpleasant sensory and emotional experience associated with, or resembling that associated with, actual or potential tissue damage.”
agr12: International Association for the Study of Pain (IASP), 2020. The six notes added to the definition:
agr14: Pain is always a personal experience that is influenced to varying degrees by biological, psychological and social factors.
agr15: It is not the same as the signal
agr16: Pain and the danger signals carried by nerves are different things. Pain cannot be inferred solely from activity in sensory nerves.
agr18: Through their life experiences, people learn the concept of pain.
agr20: A person’s report of an experience as pain should be respected.
agr21: It protects, but can also harm
agr22: Pain usually serves a protective role; but it may have adverse effects on function and on social and psychological well-being.
agr24: Describing it in words is only one of several ways to express pain; being unable to communicate does not mean there is no pain.
agr27: Pain can be compared to a fire alarm: the same smoke makes a sensitively set alarm ring much louder. Choose the factors below and see how the sound of the alarm changes. This is a teaching analogy; the numbers are illustrative and do not measure your pain.

agr39: The alarm is at roughly the same level as the incoming signal.
agr40: The same signal makes a louder sound in a sensitised alarm. The pain is real; but the tissue is not more damaged.
agr41: The calming factors turn the alarm down. The tissue is the same; but the brain perceives less danger.

agr63: So is my pain all in my head?
agr64: No. Pain is always a real experience. According to the International Association for the Study of Pain’s definition, a person’s report of pain should be respected. The fact that pain is produced in the brain does not mean it is “in your head” or made up; all pain is produced in the brain.
agr65: Does pain always mean there is damage?
agr66: Not always. Pain and the danger signal from the tissues are not the same thing; how much it hurts does not always reflect how much damage there is. For example, disc changes are very common on the lower back MRIs of people without any pain.
agr67: My MRI report mentions a herniation or degeneration. Is that the cause of my pain?
agr68: It may be, but not necessarily. These findings are common in people without pain and increase with age. Your doctor interprets the MRI together with your examination findings and symptoms.
agr70: In a review of 12 randomised trials, pain neuroscience education on its own brought only small improvements in pain and daily function; but it meaningfully reduced the fear of movement in the short term. Patients found education more helpful when they were able to tell their own story.
